title: The week-old service runs out of heap
hook: A Java service throws OutOfMemoryError after a week. Heap dumps show millions of entries in a static HashMap cache.
context: Production service whose cache keys are request-derived strings
solution_brief: The static map retains strong references indefinitely. Use an explicit bounded cache with eviction; a LinkedHashMap access-order LRU is a small single-process option. WeakHashMap is not a size bound and fails if keys stay strongly referenced elsewhere. Confirm retained size and load behavior.

steps.prompt: The heap dump shows millions of entries in CACHE, and the heap only ever grows. What is keeping that memory alive?

options.text: The static map keeps every entry reachable and never removes any
The garbage collector does not scan objects held in static fields
Request strings are interned, and interned strings are never collected

steps.explanation: A static field is a garbage-collection root, so everything the map references stays reachable, and nothing ever takes entries out. The collector does scan statics, which is exactly why it keeps their contents. Strings built from a request are not interned unless code calls intern().
steps.bottleneck_note: Anything reachable from a static field lives as long as the class does.
steps.code_snippet:
static final Map<String, Result> CACHE = new HashMap<>();
CACHE.put(requestKey, result);

steps.prompt: Why is WeakHashMap still not a safe fix for this cache?

options.text: It removes an entry only once its key is unreachable, which caps nothing
It holds its values as weak references, so cached results vanish at once
It keeps at most 16 entries, so almost every lookup will miss

steps.explanation: WeakHashMap drops an entry when nothing else references its key, which depends on who holds the key and when the collector runs, not on a size you choose. If anything keeps the keys alive, it grows just as before. Its values are ordinary strong references, and 16 is only its starting capacity.
steps.bottleneck_note: Weak keys tie an entry's life to its key's reachability, not to a size limit.
steps.context_note: A teammate proposes a one-line fix: change new HashMap<>() to new WeakHashMap<>().

steps.prompt: Which standard-library approach caps the cache at 10,000 entries and evicts the least recently used one?

options.text: A ConcurrentHashMap created with an initial capacity of 10,000
A HashMap, with System.gc() called whenever it passes 10,000

steps.explanation: With access order switched on, LinkedHashMap keeps entries from least to most recently used, and removeEldestEntry lets you drop the oldest once size() passes 10,000. A ConcurrentHashMap's initial capacity only sizes its table; it still grows without limit. System.gc() cannot free entries the map still references.
steps.bottleneck_note: Initial capacity is a sizing hint; only an eviction rule is a limit.
steps.context_note: The team agrees to cap the cache at 10,000 entries. It lives in one JVM and is not shared between hosts.

steps.prompt: After key.setTenant("other"), cache.get(key) returns null, even though the entry was put with that same object. Why?

options.text: The key's hashCode changed, so get looks in a different bucket
HashMap copies the key on put, so the change never reaches the map
Changing the key made HashMap evict the entry it belonged to

steps.explanation: HashMap picks a bucket from the key's hashCode when you call put. If fields that hashCode reads change afterwards, get computes a different hash and searches the wrong bucket, so the entry is stranded. HashMap stores a reference to your key, not a copy, which is exactly why changing it breaks the lookup.
steps.bottleneck_note: Map keys must never change the fields that equals and hashCode depend on.
steps.context_note: To speed up lookups, the String key is replaced by a Key object with setter methods.

steps.prompt: Which test shows that the leak is fixed without making the service slow?

options.text: A day-long load test watching post-GC heap, hit rate and latency
One request per endpoint, checking each returns 200 within budget
A short load test that calls System.gc() and checks used heap drops
A unit test asserting the map never holds more than 10,000 entries

steps.explanation: The leak took a week to show, so the test must run long enough for growth to appear, and heap measured after collection shows what is really retained. Hit rate and latency catch the opposite failure: a cap so small that the cache thrashes. A unit test proves the size limit, but not the memory or the speed under real traffic.
steps.bottleneck_note: A leak fix is proven over time and under load, not by one request.
steps.context_note: The bounded cache is now running in staging.
